facts.fact: At the First Battle of Panipat (1526) Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi.
Babur descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's.
Babur captured Kabul in 1504.
Babur wrote the Baburnama in Chagatai Turkish.
Babur introduced the Charbagh garden to India.
At Khanwa (1527) Babur defeated Rana Sanga.
At Chanderi (1528) Babur defeated Medini Rai.
At Ghaghra (1529) Babur defeated the Afghan confederacy.
At Panipat Babur used artillery and the tulughma (linked-cart) tactic.
Humayun divided the empire among his brothers Kamran, Askari and Hindal.
Sher Shah defeated Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540).
Humayun spent his exile at the Safavid court of Shah Tahmasp.
Humayun recaptured Delhi in 1555.
Sher Shah's original name was Farid Khan; he was titled Sher Khan for killing a tiger.
Sher Shah was born to an Afghan family at Sasaram in Bihar.
Sher Shah introduced the silver rupiya and restored the Grand Trunk Road.
Sher Shah's state share was one-third of the produce, with patta and kabuliyat.
Peasants received a patta (title deed) and signed a kabuliyat (agreement).
Sher Shah used dagh (branding) and chehra (descriptive roll).
Sher Shah standardised the copper dam.
Akbar came to the throne in 1556 at the age of thirteen.
Bairam Khan was Akbar's regent.
Akbar's side won the Second Battle of Panipat (1556) against Hemu.
Haldighati (1576) was fought against Maharana Pratap of Mewar.
The Dahsala/Zabti system used the average produce and prices of ten years.
Mansabdari ranks had two numbers, Zat and Sawar.
Akbar abolished jizya and founded the Din-i-Ilahi.
Todar Mal was the finance minister behind the revenue reforms.
Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama.
Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan translated the Baburnama into Persian.
Tansen was the renowned court musician.
Nur Jahan wielded great political influence under Jahangir.
Sir Thomas Roe visited Jahangir and secured trading rights for the English.
The English set up their first factory at Surat in 1613.
Shah Jahan's original name was Prince Khurram.
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal.
The Peacock Throne was made in Shah Jahan's reign.
Aurangzeb imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort.
Aurangzeb defeated and executed his brother Dara Shikoh.
Aurangzeb re-imposed jizya in 1679.
Aurangzeb annexed Bijapur and Golconda in 1686–87.
Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 and took the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor.
The Sayyid Brothers were king-makers of the later Mughals.
Farrukhsiyar was the first Mughal emperor killed by his own nobles.
Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh became effectively independent.
Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.
Shivaji's council of eight ministers was the Ashtapradhan.
Shivaji killed Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh (1659).
Shivaji signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Jai Singh.
Chauth was one-fourth of revenue and Sardeshmukhi an additional one-tenth.
Shahu appointed Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa in 1713.
The Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) to Ahmad Shah Abdali.
Shivaji coined the ideal of 'Hindavi Swarajya'.
Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort (1630).
Shivaji raided Surat in 1664.
Aurangzeb was called 'Zinda Pir'.
Aurangzeb appointed muhtasibs (censors of morals).
Aurangzeb executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675).
The Ain-i-Akbari is the third volume of the Akbarnama.
Sher Shah's reforms became the base for Akbar's administration.
Humayun's Tomb is India's first garden tomb.
Jahangir set up the Zanjir-i-Adl (chain of justice) at Agra Fort.
Jahangir lost Qandahar to Persia in 1622.
Akbar promoted Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all).
Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal, was exiled after the 1857 Revolt.
Babur was born in 1483 at Andijan in the Ferghana valley.
Babur became ruler of Ferghana in 1494 at the age of about eleven, after his father Umar Sheikh Mirza died.
Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of Punjab, and Rana Sanga invited Babur to invade India.
The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526.
The Battle of Khanwa (17 March 1527) was fought near Fatehpur Sikri; after it Babur took the title Ghazi.
At Ghaghra (6 May 1529) Babur defeated the Afghans under Mahmud Lodi.
Babur made Agra his capital; he died there in 1530 and was later reburied at Bagh-e-Babur in Kabul.
The Babri Masjid at Ayodhya was built in 1528 by Mir Baqi, a noble of Babur.
Aram Bagh (Ram Bagh) at Agra is one of the earliest Mughal charbagh gardens.
Humayun besieged Kalinjar in Bundelkhand in 1531.
At Dadrah (Daurah, 1532) Humayun defeated the Afghans under Mahmud Lodi near the Gomti.
Humayun drove Bahadur Shah of Gujarat out of Mandu and Champaner (1535); Bahadur Shah took refuge at Diu.
After Chausa a water-carrier named Nizam saved Humayun and was allowed to sit on the throne briefly.
In 1555 Humayun won the battles of Machhiwara and Sirhind against the Surs (Sikandar Shah Suri).
Humayun built the city of Din-panah at Delhi (on the site of the later Purana Qila).
Humayun died in 1556 after falling from the stairs of his library (Sher Mandal).
Humayun's Tomb was designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and built by his widow Bega Begum.
Gulbadan Begum, Humayun's half-sister, wrote the Humayun-nama.
Khwandamir wrote the Qanun-i-Humayuni (Humayun-nama of Khwandamir) on Humayun's early reign.
Sher Shah defeated the Lohani chiefs and the Sultan of Bengal at Surajgarh (1534).
Sher Shah died in 1545 from a gunpowder explosion while besieging Kalinjar.
Sher Shah divided his empire into 47 sarkars.
In a sarkar the Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran kept law and order and the Munsif-i-Munsifan supervised revenue and justice.
In the pargana the Amin assessed land revenue, the Fotedar was treasurer and the Karkun the accountant.
Sher Shah classified land as good, middling and bad.
Sher Shah restored the road from Sonargaon (Bengal) to Peshawar, later called the Grand Trunk Road.
Sher Shah built the Rohtas Fort in Punjab.
Sher Shah's tomb at Sasaram (Bihar) stands in the middle of a lake.
Sher Shah built the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque in the Purana Qila, Delhi.
Malik Muhammad Jayasi wrote the Padmavat in the time of Sher Shah.
Islam Shah (1545–1553), son of Sher Shah, succeeded him.
Muhammad Adil Shah Sur (1553–1555) had Firoz Shah Suri killed; his minister was Hemu.
Humayun is said to have called Sher Shah the 'teacher of kings' (Ustad-i-Badshahan) for his administration.
Akbar was born in 1542 at Umarkot in Sindh, during Humayun's flight.
Hemu took the title Vikramaditya after capturing Delhi, before losing at Second Panipat (1556).
Akbar dismissed his regent Bairam Khan in 1560.
The brief dominance of Akbar's foster-mother Maham Anaga (1560–62) is called the 'petticoat government'.
Akbar abolished the pilgrim tax in 1563 and the jizya in 1564.
Akbar built the Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 for religious debates.
The Mahzar (1579) declared Akbar the final arbiter (Imam-i-Adil) in religious disputes.
Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of the Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti.
Asirgarh (1601) was Akbar's last conquest.
Akbar annexed Kashmir in 1586.
In 1574 Akbar appointed karoris to collect revenue and check local figures.
The Dahsala system was introduced in 1580.
Under Akbar land was classed as polaj, parauti, chachar and banjar by how often it was cultivated.
Kankut was a rough estimate of the crop on the field; batai (ghalla-bakhshi) was crop-sharing.
Akbar gave peasants loans called taccavi.
Khalisa was land whose revenue went directly to the imperial treasury.
A jagir was a revenue assignment given instead of a cash salary.
Akbar divided the empire into 12 subas (later 15).
The Mir Bakhshi headed the military department and the mansabdars.
The Sadr-us-Sudur looked after religious affairs and grants.
The Mir Saman was in charge of the imperial household and karkhanas.
In a sarkar the Faujdar kept law and order and the Amalguzar collected revenue.
Late in Akbar's reign the highest mansab for nobles rose from 5,000 to 7,000.
Tansen was given the title 'Mian' by Akbar.
Birbal (Mahesh Das) was given the title Raja; he died fighting the Yusufzais (1586).
The Persian translation of the Mahabharata made under Akbar is called the Razmnama.
Daswanth and Basawan were leading painters of Akbar's court.
The Hamzanama was the first great illustrated manuscript of Akbar's studio.
Badauni's Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh criticises Akbar's religious policy.
Nizamuddin Ahmad wrote the Tabaqat-i-Akbari.
The Tarikh-i-Alfi, a history of a thousand years of Islam, was begun under Akbar.
The Jesuit Antonio Monserrate came to Akbar's court (1578–82).
Ralph Fitch was the first Englishman to describe Akbar's India (1585–91).
Prince Khusrau rebelled against Jahangir in 1606.
Jahangir had Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Sikh Guru, executed in 1606 for blessing Khusrau.
Captain William Hawkins visited Jahangir's court (1608–11).
At Swally (1612) the English under Thomas Best defeated the Portuguese near Surat.
Jahangir wrote his memoirs, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, in Persian.
Ustad Mansur, the great painter of birds and animals, worked for Jahangir.
Abul Hasan (Nadir-uz-Zaman) and Bishandas were painters of Jahangir; Bishandas was known for portraits.
Nur Jahan built the tomb of her father Itimad-ud-Daulah at Agra, the first Mughal building with pietra dura in white marble.
Akbar's tomb at Sikandra (Agra) was completed by Jahangir.
Jahangir laid out the Shalimar Bagh in Kashmir.
Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra in 1628 after defeating his brother Shahryar.
Ustad Ahmad Lahori is credited as the chief architect of the Taj Mahal.
Shah Jahan founded Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi) with the Red Fort, completed in 1648.
The Peacock Throne was made under the goldsmith Bebadal Khan.
Abdul Hamid Lahori wrote the Padshahnama, the official history of Shah Jahan.
Shah Jahan expelled the Portuguese from Hugli in 1632.
Shah Jahan regained Qandahar in 1638 but lost it finally to Persia in 1649.
Shah Jahan's Balkh campaign (1646–47) against the Uzbeks failed to hold Central Asia.
Dara Shikoh translated 50 Upanishads into Persian as the Sirr-i-Akbar and wrote the Majma-ul-Bahrain.
Aurangzeb defeated Dara Shikoh at Samugarh (1658), after Dharmat.
Tavernier and Bernier (French) and Manucci (Italian) visited Mughal India in the time of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.
François Bernier was a French physician who wrote 'Travels in the Mughal Empire'.
Aurangzeb took the title 'Alamgir' (world-conqueror).
Aurangzeb banned the Nauroz festival and stopped the weighing of the emperor (tuladan) and the jharokha darshan.
The Fatawa-i-Alamgiri, a digest of Islamic law, was compiled under Aurangzeb.
Saqi Mustaid Khan wrote the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, history of Aurangzeb's reign.
The Bibi-ka-Maqbara at Aurangabad, tomb of Aurangzeb's wife Rabia Durrani, was built by their son Azam Shah and is called the 'Taj of the Deccan'.
Aurangzeb built the Badshahi Mosque at Lahore and the Moti Masjid in the Red Fort, Delhi.
The Ahoms under Lachit Borphukan defeated the Mughals at Saraighat (1671).
Shaista Khan took Chittagong from the Arakanese (Magh pirates) in 1666.
The Jat revolt of 1669 was led by Gokula; the Satnamis rose in 1672.
Durgadas Rathore led the Rathor resistance in Marwar after 1679.
Aurangzeb died at Ahmednagar in 1707 and is buried at Khuldabad.
Bahadur Shah I (1707–1712), also called Muazzam or Shah Alam I, released Shahu.
Jahandar Shah (1712–1713) introduced ijara (revenue farming) and abolished jizya.
Farrukhsiyar's farman of 1717 gave the English duty-free trade in Bengal.
Muhammad Shah (1719–1748) was called 'Rangeela'.
Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) invaded India several times between 1748 and 1767.
Alamgir II (1754–1759) was emperor at the time of Plassey (1757) and was murdered by his wazir.
Shah Alam II fought at Buxar (1764) and under the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the English the Diwani of Bengal.
Akbar II (1806–1837) gave Rammohan Roy the title 'Raja'.
Bahadur Shah II (Zafar) died in exile at Rangoon in 1862.
Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk founded the autonomous state of Awadh.
Murshid Quli Khan made Bengal autonomous and moved its capital to Murshidabad.
Sawai Jai Singh of Amber founded Jaipur and built astronomical observatories (Jantar Mantar) at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura.
The Jat kingdom of Bharatpur reached its height under Suraj Mal.
Martanda Varma built the independent kingdom of Travancore.
Ali Muhammad Khan founded the Rohilla state of Rohilkhand.
Shivaji captured Torna fort in 1646, at about 16.
Dadoji Kondadeo was Shivaji's guardian and tutor.
At Pavan Khind (1660) Baji Prabhu Deshpande held off Siddi Masud so Shivaji could escape from Panhala.
In 1663 Shivaji raided Shaista Khan's camp at Pune (Lal Mahal) at night.
Shivaji escaped from house arrest at Agra in 1666.
Tanaji Malusare recaptured Kondhana (Sinhagad) in 1670.
Salher (1672) was the first major Maratha victory over the Mughals in open battle.
Shivaji built the Sindhudurg sea fort as a naval base.
Samarth Ramdas was Shivaji's spiritual guide.
The Maratha guerrilla technique is called 'ganimi kava'.
In the Ashtapradhan the Peshwa was the prime minister.
The Amatya (Mazumdar) was the finance/revenue minister.
The Sachiv (Surnavis) handled royal correspondence.
The Mantri (Waqianavis) kept the king's daily records and intelligence.
The Sumant (Dabir) was the foreign minister.
The Senapati (Sar-i-Naubat) commanded the army.
The Nyayadhish was the chief justice and the Panditrao handled religious affairs.
Rajaram added the post of Pratinidhi, making the council nine.
Sambhaji was captured and executed by the Mughals in 1689.
Rajaram (1689–1700) fled to Gingee, which Aurangzeb took in 1698.
Tarabai ruled as regent for her son Shivaji II and later held Kolhapur.
Shahu defeated Tarabai at the Battle of Khed (1707).
The Treaty of Warna (1731) settled the Satara–Kolhapur split.
Baji Rao I (1720–1740) raided Delhi in 1737 and took Bassein from the Portuguese in 1739.
Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb, 1740–1761) was Peshwa at the Third Battle of Panipat.
Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath helped the Sayyid brothers depose Farrukhsiyar (1719) and won Mughal grants of chauth and sardeshmukhi for the Deccan.
